title: Glossary
markdown:
**ACK**: the TCP flag meaning the acknowledgement number is valid; generally, a message saying data arrived. (1.04, 4.03)

**Ack bitfield**: 32 bits after an ack number saying which of the previous 32 packets also arrived. (5.03)

**ARP**: the protocol that finds the MAC address for an IP address on the local network. (4.02)

**Authoritative server**: a server whose simulation is the truth; clients send only inputs. (6.01)

**Backoff**: waiting longer after each failed attempt, usually doubling. (5.04)

**Baseline**: the earlier snapshot a delta is encoded against. (6.02)

**Big-endian**: most significant byte first; the network byte order. (2.03)

**Byte stream**: what TCP delivers: bytes in order, with no message boundaries. (2.02)

**Capture filter**: a BPF expression deciding which packets are recorded. (4.01)

**Checksum**: a value computed over data to detect corruption; the Internet checksum is a one's-complement sum of 16-bit words. (2.03)

**Chunked encoding**: an HTTP body sent as hex-sized pieces ending with a zero-size chunk. (3.02)

**CIDR**: writing a network as address and prefix length, such as `192.168.1.0/24`. (1.02)

**ClientHello**: the first TLS handshake message, listing versions, cipher suites and extensions. (4.05)

**Delta compression**: sending only what changed against a baseline. (6.02)

**Display filter**: a Wireshark expression deciding which captured packets are shown. (4.01)

**DNS**: the system that turns names into addresses. (1.03)

**EtherType**: the Ethernet header field saying which protocol follows. (4.02)

**Extrapolation**: guessing a position beyond the newest snapshot from its velocity. (6.03)

**FIN**: the TCP flag meaning "I have finished sending". (1.04)

**Fixed timestep**: simulating in equal ticks regardless of frame time. (6.01)

**Fragment**: a piece of a packet or block too big to send whole. (4.02, 5.05)

**Handshake**: the opening exchange of a connection: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK for TCP. (1.04)

**Head-of-line blocking**: later data waiting for a lost earlier piece. (5.01)

**Header**: the fixed fields at the start of a packet or message. (1.01)

**IHL**: the IPv4 header length, in 32-bit words. (4.02)

**Interpolation**: blending between two snapshots around a render time in the past. (6.03)

**Jitter**: variation in delay between packets. (5.01)

**Keep-alive**: reusing an HTTP connection for several requests. (3.01)

**Lag compensation**: rewinding other players to the time the shooter saw before testing a hit. (6.05)

**Latency**: the time a packet takes to arrive; the round trip is there and back. (1.04)

**Loopback**: the address of your own machine, `127.0.0.1` or `::1`. (1.02)

**MAC address**: the six-byte hardware address of a network interface. (4.02)

**MSS**: maximum segment size, the largest TCP payload a side accepts. (1.01, 4.03)

**MTU**: the largest packet a link carries. (1.01)

**NAT**: a router rewriting private addresses and ports to its public address. (1.02)

**pcap**: the classic capture file format. (4.01)

**Port**: a 16-bit number choosing which program on a machine receives the data. (1.04)

**Prediction**: applying your own inputs immediately instead of waiting for the server. (6.04)

**Pseudo-header**: the addresses, protocol and length included in TCP and UDP checksums. (4.03)

**Quantisation**: storing a value in fewer bits at a fixed step. (6.02)

**Reconciliation**: resetting to the server's state and replaying unconfirmed inputs. (6.04)

**Retransmission**: sending data again because it, or its acknowledgement, was lost. (4.04)

**Routing table**: prefixes and next hops; the longest matching prefix wins. (1.05)

**RST**: the TCP flag that aborts a connection; in reply to a SYN, "connection refused". (4.04)

**RTO**: retransmission timeout, how long to wait for an ack before resending. (5.04)

**RTT**: round-trip time. (5.04)

**Sequence number**: a counter on each packet or byte, used to order and acknowledge. (1.04, 5.02)

**Snapshot**: the world state at one server tick. (6.02)

**SNI**: server name indication, the hostname a TLS client sends in its ClientHello. (3.05, 4.05)

**Socket**: an endpoint for sending and receiving network data. (2.01)

**Subnet mask**: the bits of an address that name the network. (1.02)

**SYN**: the TCP flag that opens a connection. (1.04)

**Tick**: one step of a fixed-timestep simulation. (6.01)

**TLS**: the protocol that encrypts and authenticates a connection; the S in HTTPS. (3.05)

**TTL**: time to live, a hop count decremented by each router. (1.05)

**UDP**: the transport that sends independent datagrams with no delivery guarantee. (1.04)
